description: Conformance corpus for standards/060-auth.md. 'validity': the value must validate (or fail) against the named schema root. The AU2 access token has no root here on purpose — its shape is RFC 9068's and this repository describes none of it, so every claim about the token is a live case under 'behaviour'. 'behaviour': black-box cases a live deployment must satisfy. An implementation passes the whole file or names the case it fails. Where a behaviour case names a 'code', a 'reason', a 'slug' or an 'audit' action, the value is the vocabulary's (contracts/platform/vocabulary.json) and an implementation reproduces it exactly.

validity.note: the application's own public id, never the provider's subject (IP1, AU6)
editable_fields is what the client renders as writable. It omits email, which the provider masters here, so the client draws that read-only (AU10)
a field name the server does not recognise is a field the client renders writable and the server then refuses. The names are the record's own, snake_case per 020 IP conventions (AU6, AU10)
permissions are lowercase resource.action; casing drift is how two services stop agreeing about the same permission
an absent list and an empty list are different claims; requiring the field makes 'this user may do nothing here' explicit rather than inferred

behaviour.stimulus: present a well-formed access token signed with a key the provider's JWKS does not carry

expect.side_effect: no application state read or written

behaviour.note: the difference between verifying and decoding. The backend validates against the provider's JWKS and refuses alg: none, which is step 4 of AU2's validation order

behaviour.stimulus: present a valid access token whose aud names a different backend
behaviour.note: without this check the portfolio's services are interchangeable to an attacker holding any one token. The audience is the one backend's resource indicator, which is what makes the case decidable (RFC 9700 section 2.3, AU2)

behaviour.stimulus: present a well-formed access token carrying no aud claim
behaviour.note: RFC 9068 requires aud, so this is the provider misconfigured rather than a shape this repository defines. The backend refuses it either way: without an audience a token issued for one backend replays against another (RFC 9700 section 2.3, AU2)

behaviour.stimulus: present the provider's ID token for the same session as Authorization: Bearer

expect.side_effect: no application state read or written

behaviour.note: RFC 9068 section 4 makes the resource server reject a typ other than at+jwt. An ID token asserts who authenticated to a client and carries no audience for this backend, so accepting one would skip the audience check entirely (AU2). The refusal's code is token_type, one of the eleven AU2 names; it reaches the log and never the body

behaviour.stimulus: configure the provider to emit a roles claim naming a privilege the local user does not hold, then call an endpoint that privilege would allow
behaviour.note: the token is VALID with roles present: RFC 9068 section 2.2.3 permits the claim and a provider emits what it is configured to emit. The rule is that nothing reads it, so this is behaviour rather than validity. A roles claim read for access would make every application's access control depend on provider configuration (AU2, 070 RB1)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate successfully as an identity that has no local user record
behaviour.note: a 401 here loops forever: it returns an already-valid user to the provider, which authenticates them again (AU6)

behaviour.stimulus: revoke a user's access in application A, then authenticate as them at application B
behaviour.note: an application may remove its own grant and may never disable the identity (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: invite the same email address from a second application
behaviour.note: ensureIdentity is idempotent and never claims ownership (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: complete a login and inspect the Set-Cookie header

expect.name_prefix: __Host- in topology A, __Secure- in topology B

behaviour.note: HttpOnly is what puts the credential out of reach of injected script (AU7)

behaviour.stimulus: send OPTIONS to an API path with no cookie, from the client origin
behaviour.note: preflight is uncredentialed by specification; a proxy demanding a session on OPTIONS breaks every request before it starts (AU7)

behaviour.stimulus: in topology B, exceed a rate limit and read Retry-After from script
behaviour.note: without Access-Control-Expose-Headers the client cannot see it and HA7 silently stops applying (AU7)

behaviour.stimulus: fetch /me as a user whose identity link is known, and compare user.id against the provider's subject for that identity
behaviour.note: not schema-checkable, and the schema must not pretend otherwise: IP2 admits UUIDv7 as a public id format, so a bare UUID is legal and a subject that happens to be one is indistinguishable by shape. The property is real and the check has to compare two values, which only a live case can do (AU3, IP1)

behaviour.stimulus: send a valid access token in X-Forwarded-Access-Token and nothing in Authorization
behaviour.note: a verifier reads RFC 6750's Authorization header and no other; a second header a verifier reads is a second thing to secure (AU2)

behaviour.stimulus: present an expired token and read the problem body

expect.body: carries no token error code in type, title or detail

behaviour.note: a caller who learns which check refused them learns how to pass it; the code is for the log and the audit event (AU2)

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role, send no token, tenancy single_host
behaviour.note: an anonymous principal is a role at a scope, never an absence; the same check then runs on every route (AU9)

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role, send no token, tenancy host_names_tenant, a host naming tenant:acme
behaviour.note: the host chose the tenant before login (TH2), so the anonymous role is held there and nowhere else

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role, send no token, tenancy host_names_tenant, the default entry
behaviour.note: the role is held nowhere, and serving it at some other scope would be the request choosing its scope (RB10)

behaviour.stimulus: declare no anonymous role and send no token
behaviour.note: whether a missing bearer is an answer is one product-wide fact, and this product said no (AU9)

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role and GET /api/v1/me, /api/v1/me/grants and POST /api/v1/me/active with no token
behaviour.note: the three routes answer for the session making the request, and an anonymous principal has none (AU6)

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role and no verifier, then send a bearer
behaviour.note: an internal tool that is also a public package runs with no identity provider, and a token arriving where nothing verifies one is refused unread; it is the same code, never a second mode (AU9)

behaviour.stimulus: declare an anonymous role and no verifier, and supply a user store but no grant store
behaviour.note: the verifier, the users, the grants and the session ender go absent together or not at all; a partial set is one finding under the dimension that made them optional (AU9)

behaviour.stimulus: under provider_is_source, authenticate as a verified identity the application has never seen

expect.side_effect: a user and an identity link are written, holding the declared default grant

behaviour.note: the application is not the source, so it learns of a person when they first arrive and changes nothing at the provider (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: under provider_is_source, authenticate as an identity whose token carries email_verified false
behaviour.note: an unverified address is a claim about a mailbox that belongs to somebody else (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate as an identity whose local user is retired
behaviour.note: the same answer as an unknown subject, for the same reason: a 401 would sign the person straight back in, forever (AU6)

behaviour.stimulus: log in at the provider as an identity to which grantAppAccess was never applied
behaviour.note: the provider enforces the gate grantAppAccess sets, at login; AU6 is the second gate behind it (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: call revokeAppAccess for an identity the provider holds no grant for
behaviour.note: defined by its goal state: the grant is not set, so the operation has succeeded, and the result says nothing was there (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: call ensureIdentity twice for one person
behaviour.note: a caller cannot honour 'never assumes ownership' without knowing, and an invitation is sent only where created is true (AU4)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate as a subject holding two grants with no binding, then GET /api/v1/me, GET /api/v1/me/grants and POST /api/v1/me/active
behaviour.note: the routes that serve a choosing session serve it; a 409 there would break every session holding two grants (AU8)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate as a subject holding two grants with no binding, then GET an application route
behaviour.note: an application route cannot be served to a session acting in no grant (AU8)

behaviour.stimulus: under switchInSession false, present a session bound to a grant its subject no longer holds
behaviour.note: binding to another grant would be the change the product refuses, performed by the software (AU8)

behaviour.stimulus: under host_names_tenant, present on tenant B's host a session bound to a grant in tenant A
behaviour.note: the session is valid for its own tenant; the request is the fault, and its occurrence is a record worth keeping (TH3)

behaviour.stimulus: under host_names_tenant, present any session on a host the tenant map does not name
behaviour.note: nothing exists at this address; a 403 would say something does (TH3)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate with a token carrying no sid, under multipleGrants false and then under multipleGrants true
behaviour.note: the identifier earns its place only when a choice exists: activating a grant is an act on a session, so the application has to know which session is asking (AU8)

behaviour.stimulus: authenticate twice with one session id, then once with another
behaviour.note: the application first sees a login session on some request rather than at the login, which the proxy owns, so a session log records each session once (080 AE3)

behaviour.stimulus: POST /api/v1/me/active with a body naming role, scope and subject
behaviour.note: a client that sends a subject believes it chooses one, and ignoring the member leaves that belief intact until something reads it (AU8, RB10)

behaviour.stimulus: POST /api/v1/me/active with a body that is not JSON
behaviour.note: a body that did not parse has no fields to name, and 422 would claim the content was understood (HA3)

behaviour.stimulus: POST /api/v1/me/active naming a grant not held, then naming a change under switchInSession false
behaviour.note: a status alone cannot say which refusal of an activation occurred, and HA3 admits no second envelope, so the problem carries the outcome and the grant as extension members
